Remainder of the name, preserving the distinctive marks of the Greek tradition.

pronunciation.approximation: 'KRATOS' — pronounce the restored form with attention to the preserved diacritics and length.

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: κράτος (krátos), 'strength, power, dominion' — the personification is the common noun made flesh, like Bía or Níkē

kin.label: Derivatives
kin.form: -kratia: dēmokratíā, aristokratíā — the word that built 'democracy'

kin.label: Indo-Iranian
kin.form: Sanskrit kratú- 'power, resolve, intelligence' (Rigveda), a proposed cognate (Pokorny)

pronunciation.note: Krátos is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the acute accent on the short penult is the one feature the ASCII 'Kratos' loses; there is no long vowel and no circumflex. In living Greek the acute was musical pitch. The name is a common noun personified — Strength — exactly as Níkē is Victory.

domains.title: Strength
domains.subtitle: Strength, Power, Sovereignty
domains.lead: Krátos is Strength enthroned beside Zeus: the personified might that executes the ruler of heaven's will. Son of Styx and Pallas, brother of Níkē, Bía, and Zelos, he dwells forever at the tyrant's right hand — and speaks Greek tragedy's bleakest doctrine: none is free but Zeus.

cards.name: Strength
cards.desc: Executive force: the power that enacts a decree once Zeus has made it — the will of heaven with hands.

cards.name: Sovereignty
cards.desc: The Greek noun behind -cracy itself: dēmokratíā, aristokratíā, autokratíā — the word that built 'democracy.'

cards.name: Unicode Restoration
cards.desc: The restoration Krátos recovers the acute pitch accent that plain ASCII kratos flattens.

cards.name: Original Attestation
cards.desc: Attested in the original script as Κράτος — Hesiod's Theogony and Aeschylus' Prometheus Bound.

symbols.name: The adamantine bonds
symbols.meaning: The unbreakable chains Hephaestus forged in ignorance and Krátos fastens without pity (Prometheus Bound)

symbols.name: The Scythian crag
symbols.meaning: The remote cliff at the world's edge where Prometheus is nailed — the geography of force's work

symbols.name: Styx, mother
symbols.meaning: The underworld river whose oath binds the gods themselves — Krátos is born of the most terrible pledge

symbols.name: The house of Zeus
symbols.meaning: His only dwelling: the permanent right, granted after the Titanomachy, to sit forever beside the ruler of Olympus

mythology.lead: Krátos has no independent mythology — no quests, no loves, no temples. His entire dossier is a genealogy, an oath, one terrible scene, and the trace of a word in epic: the binding of Prometheus, in which he is the speaking voice of power.

myths.title: The Children of Styx
myths.text: Hesiod gives Krátos his family in the Theogony (375–383): the river Styx, daughter of Ocean, bore to Pallas four children — Zelos (Rivalry), trim-ankled Níkē (Victory), Krátos (Might), and Bía (Force). They are not decorative attendants. When the Titanomachy broke out, Styx was the first of the gods to bring her children over to Zeus's side, and for that loyalty Zeus granted them a rare honor: they live with him forever, 'for he ordained that they should dwell with him always and have honor beyond the other gods' (Theogony 383–403). Hyginus (Fabulae, preface) repeats the list and calls them primos in omnibus — first among all. The myth explains something precise about Greek ideas of rule: victory, rivalry, might, and force are not Zeus's rivals but his household, bound to him by gratitude and oath.

myths.title: The Will of Zeus
myths.text: Aeschylus stages Krátos in person. At the opening of Prometheus Bound, Might and Force — Krátos and Bía — drag the defiant Titan to a crag at the world's edge, and Krátos addresses the workman Hephaestus with the play's entire thesis: Zeus is new to power and ruthless; old loyalties count for nothing; 'there is no one free except Zeus' (Prometheus Bound 50–52). Hephaestus pities Prometheus and hesitates over the hammer; Krátos has no pity to hesitate with — he only checks that the work is done. Then he leaves the stage, his task complete, and never returns: force has nothing more to say once the chain is set. The drama built the West's first portrait of power as a functionary — efficient, unpersuadable, bored by the suffering it administers — and gave the abstraction a mask the audience could boo.

myths.title: The Oath of Styx
myths.text: Krátos's mother is herself an institution. In the Theogony (775–806) Hesiod explains that when the gods must swear their most terrible oath, they swear by Styx: an Olympian pours her water, and any god who forswears lies breathless for a full year, then serves nine more years exiled from the divine company. Zeus granted her this honor precisely because her children had stood by him in the war — the oath of the gods is, literally, the reward of loyalty. So Krátos descends from the one power in the cosmos that even Zeus must respect: the pledge by which rule itself is guaranteed. The genealogy is a lesson in political theology — might and the binding oath are mother and son, because force that cannot be sworn to is only violence, and an oath that cannot be enforced is only a wish.

myths.title: The Kratos of Zeus
myths.text: Homer never names a god Krátos, yet the word haunts his Zeus like a bodyguard. When the Father of Gods and Men challenges the whole pantheon, his boast is built on the noun itself: he claims an irresistible kratos and dares the gods to hang a golden rope from heaven and pull — 'you would not drag Zeus the high counselor from heaven to earth, however hard you strove' (Iliad 8.18–27). Later, when Hera calls his supremacy tyranny, she names exactly what she fears: a power without check or counsel (Iliad 8.478–483). The epic thus keeps two registers of the same word — the kratos that is Zeus's attribute and the Krátos who is Zeus's functionary, sovereignty in heaven and Might on stage. It is the ambiguity the Greeks lived with: the same strength that holds the cosmos up holds the Titan down.

lore.syncretism: Rome had no Krátos: the personification was too specifically Aeschylean to transplant, and no Latin cult of Vis or Potestas mirrors him. His afterlife is instead linguistic and theatrical. Through the suffix -kratia the word seeded the political vocabulary of the West — dēmokratíā, aristokratíā, autokratíā, bureaucratia: 'democracy,' 'aristocracy,' 'autocracy,' 'bureaucracy' are all his name doing new work. And in 2005 Sony's God of War borrowed the name for a Spartan anti-hero — a character who shares nothing with Hesiod's functionary beyond the word, which is itself the point. Strength recognizes no genealogy: wherever power is enthroned and chains are fastened without pity, the audience still supplies the name.
lore.culturalLegacy: Krátos's cult was nonexistent, but his word built a civilization's self-description. Classical Athens put his name in its constitution — dēmokratíā, the kratos of the dēmos — the same word, with the master changed, that Aeschylus' Krátos had claimed exclusively for Zeus. Every modern -cracy, from democracy to bureaucracy, descends from a god no city ever worshipped. Prometheus Bound, meanwhile, has been read in every age as an anatomy of state violence — by the Romantic rebels, by the generation of Marx, by modern stages that costume Krátos in a uniform. The personification without a temple turned out to have the largest parish of all: everyone who has felt the chain tighten knows exactly who is speaking.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Krátos is the honest god. The Greeks gave altars to Victory, Rivalry, and even Rumor, but none to Might alone — because everyone already served it. His entire theology fits in one stage direction: he enters with the chains, supervises the fastening, checks the work, and leaves. Force, Aeschylus understood, has no second act; it does not argue, does not explain, does not stay to watch.

Yet the tradition keeps returning to him with unease, and that unease is the legacy. When Athens named its constitution dēmokratia — the kratos of the demos — it answered the tyrant's Krátos in his own vocabulary: same word, opposite master. Every generation since has rehearsed the argument. Is power legitimate when it calls itself the people? Is the chain just when the decree was voted? Krátos asks nothing and answers nothing; he stands at the cliff with the hammer, waiting to see who gives the order.

lore.archaeology: No temple, image, or votive of Krátos is attested; his entire material record is textual. The binding of Prometheus was a favorite of Attic vase painters from the sixth century BCE — Hephaestus strapping the Titan to the crag, the Oceanids wringing their hands — but the painters show the smith, not Might; the pairing of Krátos and Bía belongs to Aeschylus' stage, and papyri of Prometheus Bound from Roman Egypt are the god's only 'sites.' Even his mother left barely a footprint: Styx was honored at a single Arcadian spring and a hill in Elis (Pausanias 8.17–18) — a fitting inheritance for the family of oaths: real, but rarely visited.
